🔔 Ethereum price holds above $1,750 after 12% rally as bulls battle key resistance 

🔖 Ethereum has climbed about 12% since July 1 as weaker-than-expected U.S. employment data and renewed institutional inflows pushed buyers back into the market, although the asset now faces heavy resistance near the $1,800 level. Ethereum’s rally gathered pace after the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics reported that June nonfarm payrolls rose by just 57,000, far below expectations of roughly 115,000. Treasury yields also eased following the release, giving cryptocurrencies another tailwind as investors rotated back into higher-beta assets.

⚠️ Ethereum’s own fundamentals strengthened alongside the macro backdrop. On July 1, Ethereum Institutional launched with backing from ecosystem leaders including co-founder Joe Lubin to accelerate institutional adoption of the network. A day later, U.S. spot Ethereum ETFs reversed an eight-week streak of net outflows, attracting $29.1 million in fresh capital led by BlackRock’s ETHA. The return of positive ETF flows removed a persistent source of selling pressure that had weighed on ETH throughout the second quarter. 

🌐 Ethereum entered the rebound from deeply oversold conditions after closing its first-ever stretch of three consecutive losing quarters. The correction dragged ETH from above $3,400 to nearly $1,563 by July 1 while active network addresses fell roughly 46%, leaving market positioning heavily skewed toward bearish bets before buyers regained control. The daily chart shows ETH reclaiming the 0.786 Fibonacci retracement near $1,704 after bouncing from the $1,500 region. Price is also pressing against the daily Supertrend resistance around $1,807 while remaining beneath a descending trendline that has capped every rally since May.

📰 Bushehr: The Nuclear Plant That Was Struck, And Wasn’t

An Iranian deputy governor in Bushehr province told state media that “several points,” including the area around the Bushehr nuclear power plant, were hit in the latest U.S. strikes.

Iranian TV reported that an American projectile landed near the facility, and a few hours later there were more explosions reported in its vicinity. 

Almost simultaneously, other Iranian outlets insisted there had been no strike on the Bushehr plant itself, and none on Kharg Island either.

That contradiction isn’t bad translation. It’s policy. Opposition-linked Iranian channels say the blasts in the province came from an attack on a “secret” Revolutionary Guards air base — a site that, by definition, does not officially exist and therefore cannot be “hit” in any authorized narrative. 

Pro-regime voices, meanwhile, need the nuclear site to appear under threat enough to justify anger and retaliation, but not so damaged that Iran looks naked and incompetent.

Israeli media took the opposite route: they published footage under headlines like “Strike on Iran’s Bushehr nuclear power plant,” then added breathless notes that a U.S. radioactive particle collection aircraft had crossed the Atlantic, proof (they implied) that nuclear facilities were now firmly in the crosshairs. 

Reports of strikes also surfaced near Isfahan, home to another nuclear-related site, further feeding the sense that the atom, not just the coastline, is in play.

Iran denies a hit on the plant so it doesn't look exposed, and confirms hits "near" it so escalation stays justified.  

Supporters abroad — whether cheering Washington or cheering Tehran — pick the version that fits their own storyline. The nuclear program itself remains the one thing everyone talks about, waves around in speeches, and uses to scare markets, while almost nobody claims to have actually seen damage to the core.

In this war, Bushehr is less a building and more a talking point: a place that’s always “almost” struck, “nearly” contaminated, “possibly” targeted — forever close enough to sell fear, never clear enough to admit what really happened.
